questions.q: Why does Halvorsen's architect recommend staying single-org rather than splitting off a separate EU org for VAT reporting?
options: Because Salesforce does not allow more than one org per company
Because the VAT requirement needs the right fields and reporting on a single org's data, not separate data residency, so a second org would solve a problem Halvorsen doesn't actually have
Because multi-org strategies are never appropriate for distributors
Because VAT reporting is not a real regulatory requirement
questions.explain: The case study's point is that a regulatory reporting requirement doesn't automatically require a separate org — it requires the right fields and reports on the existing model. Splitting into a second org would be solving a data-residency problem Halvorsen doesn't have in this scenario.

questions.q: Why did Halvorsen's architect choose a lookup relationship instead of master-detail from Order to Account?
options: Lookup relationships are always faster regardless of data shape
Orders don't need to inherit Account's sharing or be deleted when the Account is deleted, and master-detail risked concentrating skew on large distributor accounts
Master-detail relationships are deprecated on the Salesforce platform
Lookup relationships support more fields than master-detail
questions.explain: The architect's reasoning combines two things: Orders don't need master-detail's cascading-delete/sharing-inheritance behavior, and with 60 million Orders against 11 million Accounts, master-detail would risk parent-account skew concentrating on Halvorsen's largest distributor accounts.

questions.q: What problem does archiving closed Orders older than three years into a Big Object solve in this case study?
options: It deletes the data permanently to free up storage
It keeps old Orders queryable for rare audits while removing their volume from the primary object's active-record footprint and day-to-day query performance
It automatically converts Orders into Opportunities
It removes the need for any VAT reporting at all
questions.explain: The archiving cutoff keeps data available for the rare case it's needed (an older VAT audit) without that volume continuing to slow down everyday queries and reports on the primary Order object.

questions.q: What specifically made naive master-detail from Order to Account a skew risk in Halvorsen's scenario?
options: A handful of large distributor accounts could end up owning hundreds of thousands of child Orders each, concentrating lock contention during bulk updates
Master-detail relationships cannot be created on the Order object
Skew only matters for lookup relationships, not master-detail
Halvorsen has too few Account records for skew to be a concern
questions.explain: With 60 million Orders against only 11 million Accounts, a small number of large distributor accounts could realistically accumulate disproportionate Order counts, creating exactly the kind of parent-record lock contention that skew describes.

questions.q: What distinguishes a real architecture case-study write-up from a generic best-practices list, per this lesson?
options: Using the most technical vocabulary possible
Each recommendation tying back to one of the company's actual numbers or actual constraints
Avoiding any mention of specific business requirements
Recommending the same three decisions regardless of the company's situation
questions.explain: The lesson's write-up ties staying single-org, choosing lookup over master-detail, and the archiving cutoff each back to a specific Halvorsen requirement or number — that traceability from decision to concrete constraint is what makes it a real recommendation rather than a generic checklist.
